paragraphs.text: Pesachim 66b: ‘Rabbi Mani bar Patish said: Whoever becomes angry, even if greatness has been apportioned to him from heaven, he is lowered from his greatness. From where do we derive this? From Eliab, David’s older brother, as it is stated: “And Eliab’s anger burned against David and he said: Why did you come down, and with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your insolence and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle” (I Samuel 17:28); we see that Eliab became angry. And when Samuel went to anoint him after God had told him that one of Yishai’s sons was to be the king, concerning all of the other brothers it is written: “The Lord has not chosen this…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Pesachim 66b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“[for every sin exists in potential before actualization, as seen in Eliab: "for I have rejected him," our Sages noting (Pesachim 66b) this was due to his anger at David, which occurred later in time, the potential...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 66b: ‘Rabbi Mani bar Patish said: Whoever becomes angry, even if greatness has been apportioned to him from heaven, he is lowered from his greatness. From where do we derive this? From Eliab, David’s older brother, as it is stated: “And Eliab’s anger burned against David and he said: Why did you come down, and with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your insolence and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle” (I Samuel 17:28); we see that Eliab became angry. And when Samuel went to anoint him after God had told him that one of Yishai’s sons was to be the king, concerning all of the other brothers it is written: “The Lord has not chosen this…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 18, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Pesachim 66b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“and as stated in Pesachim 66b on "for I have rejected him"—implying Eliab had previously been eligible, proving kingship belonged to Jesse's sons, a father meriting for his son [as noted in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu 20...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 89b: ‘We learned in the mishna: From where is it derived that one ties a scarlet strip of wool to the scapegoat? As it says: “If your sins be like scarlet [kashanim], they will become white like snow” (Isaiah 1:18). The Gemara wonders at this: Why does the verse use the plural form: Kashanim?
